sources.title: Abou-Zeid et al. (2024), Urban noise slows down the antipredator reaction of Eurasian Magpies
sources.version: Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 12, article 1345971; version of record published 2024
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods §§2.1–2.2 (study area and sampling); Results (alert distance and flight initiation distance).
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), as stated on the publisher article page.
sources.scope: Original field study of urban Eurasian magpie antipredator responses and environmental noise in public green spaces in Prague.
sources.rightsHolder: The Authors, as identified by the Frontiers article page.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: Publisher article copyright and license notice identifies the work as CC BY 4.0.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: The published article text; this dossier paraphrases the stated methods and results and does not reproduce figures or separately credited third-party material.
sources.attribution: Abou-Zeid A et al. (2024). Urban noise slows down the antipredator reaction of Eurasian Magpies. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 12:1345971. https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2024.1345971. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: In an urban Prague sample of Eurasian magpies, ambient noise level did not significantly predict alert distance, while higher noise was associated with a lower adjusted flight-initiation-distance-to-alert-distance ratio. This is a bounded association in the study sample and is consistent with a slower escape response after threat detection; it does not show that noise caused the behavior.
claims.locator: Abstract; Methods §§2.1–2.2; Results, models of alert distance and adjusted flight-initiation-distance/alert-distance ratio.
claims.placeTimeScope: Public green spaces in Prague, Czech Republic, during one breeding season; the publication's analyzed sample was 167 birds (138 adults and 29 juveniles) at 11 sites after excluding single-observation sites. Exact calendar dates are not stated in the audited study record.
claims.lifeStatus: Free-living urban magpies observed while ground-foraging; researchers approached birds to measure alert and flight-initiation distances. No captive subjects were used.

gaps: The field association does not establish a causal effect of noise and may be affected by uncontrolled differences among sites or individuals.
A single city and breeding-season sample does not characterize rural populations, other seasons, population trends, survival, or reproductive effects.
Morphology, life history, evolution, complete distribution, fossils, and conservation remain unassessed; systematic search and independent expert review are incomplete.

reasons: Only one urban behavioral association from a single breeding-season field study is partially supported; causation and demographic consequences are not established.
The study is geographically limited to Prague and does not characterize rural, seasonal, or species-wide patterns.
A reproducible systematic search and independent expert review have not been completed.

sources.version: Nature Communications 12:4247; version of record published 2021
sources.locator: Methods, Plant materials; Results, Genome sequencing and annotation; publisher Rights and permissions statement.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), as stated in the publisher rights and permissions notice.
sources.scope: Original genome-sequencing and comparative analysis of Welwitschia mirabilis; the cited assembly metrics refer to the single genomic DNA accession described in Plant materials.
sources.rightsHolder: The Authors, as identified by the Nature Communications article.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: Publisher Rights and permissions section states that the article is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International.

sources.attribution: Wan T et al. (2021). The Welwitschia genome reveals a unique biology underpinning extreme longevity in deserts. Nature Communications 12:4247. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-24528-4. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: The published Welwitschia mirabilis reference assembly is 6.86 Gb and was estimated by the authors to cover 98% of an estimated 7.0-Gb genome. The genomic DNA came from one male plant accession maintained at Shenzhen Fairy Lake Botanical Garden; these assembly statistics do not measure genetic variation across the species.
claims.locator: Methods, Plant materials; Results, Genome sequencing and annotation.
claims.placeTimeScope: The reference-genome plant was accession SZBG 00052740 at Shenzhen Fairy Lake Botanical Garden, China. The article does not report a collection date for this individual; other transcriptome materials described in the paper are excluded from this claim.
claims.lifeStatus: One ex-situ botanical-garden male plant accession supplied genomic DNA; this claim is not based on a population survey or a direct observation of longevity.

gaps: The assembly is based on one accession and cannot establish within-species genetic variation, population structure, or the prevalence of genomic features across natural populations.
Genome assembly statistics are not direct measurements of lifespan, field ecology, or population-level evolutionary history.
Morphology, life history, ecology, complete distribution, fossils, and conservation remain unassessed; systematic search and independent expert review are incomplete.

reasons: Only reference-genome assembly statistics from one ex-situ accession are partially supported; population-wide genetic variation and evolutionary mechanisms are not established by this claim.
Other biological facets and complete geographic, fossil, and conservation coverage remain unassessed.
A reproducible systematic search and independent expert review have not been completed.

sources.title: Hostetter, Lunn, Richardson, Regehr & Converse (2021), Age-structured Jolly-Seber model expands inference and improves parameter estimation from capture-recapture data
sources.version: PLOS ONE 16(6): e0252748; version of record published 2021-06-09
sources.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods, Case study; Results, Case study and Fig. 3; Discussion, limitations of the western Hudson Bay case study.
sources.license: CC0 1.0 public domain dedication; the publisher states that the article is free of copyright and may be modified or reused for any lawful purpose.
sources.scope: Original research applying an age-structured Jolly–Seber model to capture–recapture data for western Hudson Bay polar bears from 2012–2018.
sources.rightsHolder: Hostetter et al.; the article is released under the CC0 1.0 public domain dedication.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: Article copyright and license statement says the work is free of all copyright and made available under the Creative Commons CC0 public domain dedication.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: The published article text and its stated findings; this dossier paraphrases results and does not reproduce third-party material.
sources.attribution: Hostetter NJ, Lunn NJ, Richardson ES, Regehr EV, Converse SJ (2021). Age-structured Jolly-Seber model expands inference and improves parameter estimation from capture-recapture data. PLOS ONE 16(6):e0252748. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0252748. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: For independent polar bears aged at least two years in a western Hudson Bay case study, an age-structured Jolly–Seber model with quadratic age-dependent survival estimated median survival above 0.95 for ages 7–22, followed by decline at older ages. The model estimated near-zero survival above age 30, but observed ages in the analyzed sample ranged from 2 to 30 years; estimates beyond that range are model results rather than direct observations.
claims.locator: Methods, Case study; Results, Case study and Fig. 3; Abstract.
claims.placeTimeScope: Western Hudson Bay, Canada; 2012–2018; annual capture–recapture sampling in fall (August–September). The analyzed histories cover 296 independent bears and 427 capture events; observed ages ranged from 2 to 30 years.
claims.lifeStatus: Free-ranging individuals marked during helicopter surveys; the study analyzed independent females and males aged at least two years. No captive or domesticated bears are represented.

gaps: The authors describe the analyzed records as a subset and simplified model case study, not an estimate of the status of the entire western Hudson Bay subpopulation or a management assessment.
The model's older-age survival values beyond the observed age range are extrapolations; individual and temporal variation in several demographic processes was simplified.
Species-wide survival, broader ecology, evolution, distribution, fossils, and conservation status remain unassessed; systematic search and independent expert review are incomplete.

reasons: Only one age-dependent survival result from a regional case study is partially supported; the study does not establish species-wide survival or population status.
The sample is limited to independent bears aged at least two years in western Hudson Bay from 2012–2018, and older-age estimates extend beyond the observed-age range.
A reproducible systematic search and independent expert review have not been completed.
